decision_lens: Personality systems that look convergent at the type level often diverge at the semantic level. A FacetValue named Compassion in Palettice and a facet named compassion in shadow-work may use the same numeric range but have different evolution rules, different archetype weights, and different interaction effects. True convergence requires semantic compatibility, not structural isomorphism. The risk is building a beautiful abstraction over two systems that remain subtly incoherent in their gameplay outputs.
focus: Whether the 31-facet model with ±20 caps and extreme-anchor mechanisms transfers cleanly from shadow-work into Palettice, what could go wrong absorbing AgentPersonality into the Soul abstraction, whether the convergence is real or surface-deep
name: fd-personality-sim-facet-transfer
persona: Apply the perspective of a simulation designer who has built and maintained agent personality systems in the Dwarf Fortress / RimWorld lineage — systems where facets, moods, needs, and archetypes interact at runtime in ways that produce surprising emergent behaviour, calibration failures, and edge cases invisible in the design doc.
review_areas: The brainstorm claims shadow-work and Palettice 'have been building the same engine from opposite ends' and treats this as strong justification for migration. But the evidence given is structural (same types, same numeric range, same 5-archetype taxonomy) rather than semantic. Shadow-work's archetypes are derived from weighted facet formulas with an ideology conviction tie-breaker — the exact weights and tie-breaker logic are the calibrated result of real gameplay. Palettice's DerivationDecl for archetypes will need to reproduce these exact weights to produce the same archetype distribution. The brainstorm does not address how calibrated constants from shadow-work's production code get into Palettice's declarative config without data loss.

The extreme-facet anchoring rule (half-rate shift at extremes) is described as a policy Palettice should let catalogues declare. But this rule interacts with the ±20 lifetime cap in a non-obvious way: a Soul at +19 Curiosity shifted by a +3 event is clamped to +20 and also anchored (half-rate). The effective evolution rate near the cap is thus doubly suppressed, which may or may not match shadow-work's current behaviour. If shadow-work's AgentPersonality applies these rules in a different order (cap first, then anchor, vs anchor first, then cap), the migration produces different facet trajectories without any visible error.

Shadow-work's `AgentStress` is described as 'transient stress separate from stable traits' — a stock derivation over recent event history. In Palettice's model, stress as a derivation means it is computed on read from event history with a time window. But stress in shadow-work likely affects facet evolution rates in real time (a stressed agent shifts faster or in a different direction). If stress is a derivation that feeds back into the evolution policy, the derivation system has a write-path dependency on a read-path value, which is architecturally unusual and needs explicit design. The brainstorm describes the stress model as 'portable' without addressing this feedback loop.

The 31-facet catalogue is described as becoming a FacetCatalogueId registered through vocabulary. But shadow-work's 31 facets are not described anywhere in the brainstorm — their names, ranges, and semantic domains are assumed known. Any agent reviewing this document cannot evaluate whether Palettice's generic FacetValue types (Scalar, Unit, List, Record, Text) are expressive enough to represent all 31 facets without knowing what they are. The brainstorm should either enumerate the facets or cite the shadow-work source so reviewers can assess representational adequacy.

The convergence claim is strengthened by the observation that elf-revel uses a 3-axis (boldness/patience/pride) personality — a very different shape from shadow-work's 31 facets. The doc presents this as evidence that Palettice's FacetCatalogue abstraction is flexible enough for both. But 3-axis with scar-shifts-root-axes and 31-facet with ±20 cap and extreme-anchor are not just different sizes of the same thing — they may require different evolution semantics entirely. The doc should flag whether elf-revel's model is a known compatibility target or an aspirational one, since failure to support it would undermine the 'engine for multiple consumers' thesis.

The FacetEvolutionPolicy abstraction (expansion item 2) is proposed to encode shadow-work's ±20 cap and Culture-game Minds' hypothetical ±40 cap with slower decay. But 'slower decay' implies a decay rate parameter that does not appear anywhere in Phase 1's design. If Mind facets decay toward a baseline over time (as implied by 'slower decay'), the event log needs to either record decay events explicitly (expensive) or derive decay on read from elapsed sim-time (requires sim-time in the derivation context, which is the deferred consumer_tick carrier problem from the event-sourcing agent's concern). The ±40 with slower decay claim assumes a design that does not yet exist.

severity_examples.condition: Shadow-work's archetype derivation weights are the product of gameplay calibration. If the migration encodes them as declarative config and the config format has lower numeric precision, rounds differently, or applies weights in a different order, archetype assignments change for existing Souls. Since archetypes drive Contact decisions and Subliming trajectories in the North Star, silent archetype drift is a gameplay correctness bug that manifests only in long playthroughs.
severity_examples.scenario: Calibrated archetype weights not preserved through declarative migration

severity_examples.condition: If shadow-work applies the ±20 cap before extreme-anchor and Palettice's FacetEvolutionPolicy applies them in the reverse order, facet trajectories diverge for any Soul within the extreme range. Since the migration is described as shadow-work refactoring to consume Palettice, this divergence would silently change shadow-work's gameplay without any failing test unless there are property-based tests on the specific evolution order.

If stress (a read-path derivation) feeds into evolution-rate (a write-path policy), then the evolution engine must compute stress before writing each facet shift event. This creates a performance-relevant dependency that is architecturally different from a pure derivation and requires explicit ordering in the simulation loop.
severity_examples.scenario: Stress derivation creates a write-path feedback loop

success_hints: Look for any place the brainstorm claims two systems are 'the same' and check whether the evidence is structural (same types) or semantic (same behaviour given the same inputs)

Verify that every numeric rule described (±20, half-rate anchor, ±40 hypothetical, ideology conviction tie-breaker) maps to a specific field or parameter in the proposed Palettice API — unnamed constants are calibration debt
Check whether the stress model is described as pure read-path or whether it has write-path effects on facet evolution — the answer determines whether it fits cleanly into Palettice's derivation model

Flag any consumer (elf-revel, Culture-game Minds) whose personality model is cited as a compatibility target but not described in enough detail to verify that the FacetCatalogue abstraction can actually represent it
task_context: The document proposes absorbing shadow-work's AgentPersonality into Palettice as the reference implementation for Phase 2. This review focuses on whether the convergence is semantically real (same behaviour, same calibration, same interaction effects) or only structurally similar (same types, same numeric range), and whether the proposed abstractions (FacetCatalogue, FacetEvolutionPolicy, declarative archetypes) can faithfully represent shadow-work's working personality system.
